title: Questions That a Strategic Plan Must Answer
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: Nickhart argues that most school improvement plans are too comprehensive because they are structured around Ofsted framework compliance rather than a genuine model of school effectiveness, and proposes five questions that any authentic strategic plan must answer. The five questions are: What are our anchoring concepts of school life? How are we communicating these to the community? What is our shared language? How will the team learn and develop? What needs improving versus what needs maintaining? His preferred anchoring concept is the Ambition Institute's model of school leadership as persistent problem-solving (Tom Rees and Jen Barker), which he argues runs coherently from classroom to system leadership. On shared language, Nickhart argues that the precision of language across tens of colleagues determines whether shared understanding or shared confusion governs daily practice—a strategic infrastructure question that most plans neglect. On team development, he argues that professional learning must be explicitly and deliberately designed across a scale of formality rather than vaguely allocated through INSET days. Critically, he argues headteachers must serve as gatekeepers of collective attention: it is not viable for all middle leaders to simultaneously push improvement in their areas, and deciding what can be maintained at current levels is as strategic as deciding where to improve.
points: Most school improvement plans are too comprehensive because they mirror the Ofsted framework rather than reflecting the school's actual strategic thinking; a comprehensive model of school leadership in leaders' heads is needed, not a comprehensive document on paper.

Anchoring concepts should organize all other school work—school leadership conceived as persistent problem-solving is a powerful anchoring concept because it runs from classroom to system leadership without contradiction.

Shared language is strategic infrastructure: when tens of colleagues work in a school daily, precision in what words mean for even everyday elements of school life determines whether shared understanding or shared confusion governs practice.

Professional learning must be explicitly designed and deliberately brokered across a scale of formality—team planning meetings and informal learning are chronically underused development systems, and vague CPD allocation substitutes for thoughtful design.

Headteachers must gatekeep collective attention: it is not viable for all middle leaders to simultaneously improve their areas; deciding what to maintain is as strategic as deciding what to improve, and is often the harder call.
quotes: Nearly every strategic plan that I have written and seen are far too comprehensive and I think the Ofsted framework has influenced this. Some strategic plans read like a checklist of what leaders are doing about every bullet point in the good descriptors for each of the areas in which Ofsted makes a judgement.

While a comprehensive school development plan is not desirable, a comprehensive model of thinking about school leadership is. It is an important distinction because what we hold in our heads may need to be translated somewhat for the rest of the community.

The precision of our language can support colleagues to develop a shared understanding of what we are trying to achieve and the strategies that we have selected to achieve them. Or indeed it can muddy the waters. Therefore I'd argue that we need to be a lot clearer about the words that we use for even the every day elements of school life.

Despite the excitement of designing the future in different anchoring concepts, none of those narratives will have a starting point of zero. Some may be further developed than others and, at different points, it will be good enough, good enough to focus on maintenance and not improvement.
Headteachers need to be the gatekeeper of collective attention, managing the expectations of each leader about what is required and when.

Many plans are operational, detailing what, who, when and at what cost which is no doubt important. I haven't written a single plan yet like that has gone as expected: new priorities emerge, staffing changes, capacity is reduced etc. Operational plans are vital but require a clearer idea of strategy to be of most use.
